links.comparator_used: Usual care: control-group doctors did not receive AI-ECG results and interpreted ECGs themselves (no automatic notification)
links.outcome: NOAC prescription within 90 days after discharge (also new AF diagnosis)
links.effect: NOAC prescription 23.3% vs 12.0% (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.11-3.07); AF diagnosis 47.8% vs 36.0% (HR 1.40, 95% CI 1.03-1.90); no significant difference in echocardiograms (HR 1.14), cardiology visits (HR 1.42, 95% CI 0.98-2.05), stroke, CV death or all-cause death
links.tradeoff: 48 vs 35 potential AI false-positive cases (AF not confirmed by cardiologist); only 1 led to NOAC prescription, which was clinically justified. AF misdiagnosis remained high (55.1% vs 68.6%), so physicians often did not act on alerts. Effect on alert fatigue was uncertain.
links.quote: The prescription rates of NOACs after discharge within 90 days after the index ECG were 23.3% in the intervention group and 12.0% in the control group, resulting in a HR of 1.85 (95% CI, 1.11–3.07).

links.comparator_used: Usual care with no access to AI-ECG results (not a passive-display arm)
links.outcome: NOAC prescription within 90 days after discharge (also new AF diagnosis)
links.effect: NOAC prescription 23.3% vs 12.0% (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.11-3.07); AF diagnosis 47.8% vs 36.0% (HR 1.40, 95% CI 1.03-1.90); no significant differences in clinical outcomes
links.tradeoff: 48 vs 35 potential AI errors; only 1 patient with a false alert received NOAC (justified). The study did not test whether alert fatigue occurred. Cardiology visits rose numerically but not significantly.
links.quote: The prescription rates of NOACs after discharge within 90 days after the index ECG were 23.3% in the intervention group and 12.0% in the control group, resulting in a HR of 1.85 (95% CI, 1.11–3.07).
